title: massive intestinal bleeding in a child with superior mesenteric artery aneurysm and gastrointestinal tuberculosis
display_name: Massive Intestinal Bleeding in a Child With Superior Mesenteric Artery Aneurysm and Gastrointestinal Tuberculosis
abstract: introduction superior mesenteric artery (sma) aneurysms are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population. they are most commonly caused by infection or inflammatory processes and typically present with acute abdominal pain (1,2). we report the case of a 12-year-old girl with gastrointestinal tuberculosis (gitb) who presented with massive lower gastrointestinal (gi) bleeding due to a bleeding sma aneurysm. to the best of our knowledge, this is the only reported case of tuberculosis associated with an sma aneurysm in a child and 1 of only 2 reports in patients of any age group (3). case report a 12-year-old african american female was transferred from an outside hospital for evaluation of a significant painless lower gi bleed of approximately 300 ml bright red blood per rectum. she reported a 2-day history of flank and back pain, and decreased appetite and oral intake. she had 3 episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious emesis and nausea. she denied fever, dysuria or diarrhea. she reported intermittent abdominal pain for the past several months that occasionally woke her from sleep. her past medical history was significant for a ruptured appendix 4 months prior. initially, she was treated conservatively with antibiotics but subsequently underwent laparoscopic appendectomy. her mother reported intermittent weight loss and gain but felt this was related to the appendicitis. there was no family history of inflammatory bowel disease, polyps or bleeding disorders. results of initial laboratory tests were as follows: white blood cell count 29,000/mm3 with 52% neutrophils, 37% bands, hemoglobin 4.7 g/dl, platelets 294,000/mm3, prothrombin time 21 , international normalized ratio of 1.6, partial thromboplastin time of 30.6 , bicarbonate 18 mmol/l, calcium of 6.4 mg/dl and an albumin of 1.8 g/dl. hemoglobin electrophoresis was normal. she was transfused 3 u of packed red blood cells and given vitamin k. blood and urine cultures were negative and stool studies for salmonella, shigella, campylobacter and clostridium difficile were negative but positive for adenovirus 40/41 and rotavirus. abdominal x-ray showed a gasless abdomen and air-fluid levels. meckel scan was negative. she was made n.p.o. and started on famotidine 20 mg iv b.i.d. the patient continued to have profuse bleeding that required transfusions of packed red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma. on hospital day 2, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (egd) and flexible sigmoidoscopy were performed. the egd was normal. the sigmoidoscopy to 40 cm showed numerous large clots in the rectum and sigmoid. the underlying mucosa seemed edematous, and there were scattered circumscribed ulcers with focal loss of the normal vascular pattern. she was started on empiric therapy with ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole, gangcyclovir and methylprednisone 20 mg iv b.i.d. for possible crohn disease and cytomegalovirus infection. a central line was placed and total parenteral nutrition initiated. pathology revealed normal antral mucosa that was helicobacter pylori negative. multiple biopsies from the sigmoid showed mild acute inflammation without granulomas, architectural distortion, ischemic changes or viral inclusions. cultures remained negative and the antibiotics were discontinued. the patient continued to have episodic bleeding of 100 to 450 ml daily. tagged red blood cell scans on hospital days 6 and 7 were negative. stool tests for adenovirus 40/41 and rotavirus were repeated and were positive. on hospital day 8, on the pediatric surgeon's recommendation, she underwent superior mesenteric arteriogram that demonstrated a small saccular aneurysm from the jejunal branch in the left upper quadrant fed by the inferior and superior mesenteric arteries with active bleeding into the small bowel (fig. 1). multiple microcoils were deployed into the sac, and the feeding branches off the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries were embolized. there were no further episodes of bleeding, and she was discharged home on hospital day 12 on a general diet with famotidine and a prednisone taper. she was given a steroid taper for a presumptive diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease based on her history of recurrent abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss and bleeding and on the biopsies that demonstrated mild acute inflammation in the sigmoid. initial immunomodulatory medications were withheld given her recent history of an extended antibiotic course for a perforated appendix and multiple intra-abdominal abscesses. we had planned to complete her work-up as an outpatient; however, she was not compliant with follow-up.fig. 1: superior mesenteric arteriogram with aneurysm (arrow) from jejunal branch in left upper quadrant.the patient returned to our pediatric emergency department 4 months later with a temperature of 38.9 c, epigastric pain, 2 episodes of hematemesis and 1 episode of hematochezia. she had completed her steroid taper 2 weeks prior. result of the laboratory tests were as follows: white blood cell count 18,500/mm3 with 60% neutrophils and 19% bands, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dl, platelets 573,000/mm3, mean corpuscular volume of 65 mc, c-reactive protein 76 ng/ml, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 54 mm/h and bicarbonate 21 mmol/l. liver function tests, amylase and lipase were normal. stool was negative for occult blood. anti-saccharomyces cerevisiae igg was 41.2 eu/ml (normal <40), anti-saccharomyces cerevisiae iga 18.8 eu/ml, perinuclear antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody negative and anti-ompc iga was 18.5 eu/ml (normal <16.5). additional family history revealed 2 grandparents with a history of intracranial aneurysms. computed tomography (ct)-angiogram of the brain showed no evidence of aneurysm formation. upper gi and small bowel follow through on hospital day 2 showed 2 irregular sinus tracts extending from the second portion of the duodenum and no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease (fig. 2). abdominal ultrasound (us) demonstrated 2 hyperechoic masses, 1 on the head and 1 on the tail of the pancreas, multiple small lymph nodes and hypoechoic tubular structures near the hilum of the liver. a purified protein derivative (ppd) skin test was placed and was 15 mm at 36 hours. upon direct questioning, the family now reported several family members with a history of tuberculosis, including one who died from related complications. however, the patient had a history of multiple negative ppd and a normal chest x-ray. chest x-ray was repeated and was without evidence of tuberculosis. gastric aspirates were positive for mycobacterium tuberculosis, and the patient was started on quadruple therapy with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. a ct performed on hospital day 8 demonstrated numerous retroperitoneal, porta hepatic, mesenteric and pericecal lymph nodes, some of which were necrotic, multiple loculated abdominal and pelvic fluid collections, intraperitoneal free fluid and bowel wall thickening with fluid-filled loops. the patient's symptoms began to abate, and she was discharged home on hospital day 10 with quadruple antituberculous therapy. she continues to be followed by the pediatric infectious disease service and is asymptomatic.fig. 2: upper gi demonstrating 2 irregular sinus tracts (arrows) extending from the second portion of the duodenum without evidence of inflammatory bowel disease.discussion this case highlights a unique presentation in the pediatric population of gastrointestinal tuberculosis causing bleeding from an sma aneurysm, presenting with a massive lower gi bleed. sma aneurysms are uncommon and even more so in pediatric patients. they are life threatening when they rupture and cause profound bleeding with mortality rates close to 50% (1). infections such as bacterial endocarditits are the most common cause of sma aneurysms in patients less than 50 years old (1). extensive review of the literature yielded only a few isolated reports of sma aneurysms in children. michalsky reported a previously healthy 12-year-old girl who presented with severe abdominal pain and emesis and who was found to have an sma aneurysm (4). she ultimately required arterial graft; however, no underlying cause of the aneurysm was identified. volpe et al reported the case of a 14-year-old girl who developed fever, abdominal pain and a precipitous drop in hemoglobin after mitral valve repair. ultrasound was suggestive of an sma aneurysm that was confirmed by surgery. her aneurysm was due to bacterial endocarditis (5). christophe et al also describe an sma aneurysm due to mitral valve disease and bacterial endocarditis in a 6-year-old girl. she presented with a slow-growing retro-umbilical mass that on laparotomy was found to be a ruptured sma aneurysm with a large intramesenteric hematoma (6). there are a limited number of reports of tuberculous aneurysms, most of which describe abdominal aortic aneurysms (7,8). the only pediatric report of a mycotic aneurysm due to tuberculosis was a 14-year-old who presented with abdominal pain, chills and weight loss and was found to have an abdominal aortic aneurysm. that patient underwent insertion of an aortic graft but died from postoperative "hypovolemia" (9). we found a single reported case of tuberculosis causing an sma aneurysm and catastrophic gi bleeding in the adult literature. oran et al described a case of a 41-year-old woman who presented massive lower gi bleed due to a mesenteric artery aneurysm caused by gitb (3). however, this patient's case was complicated by significant immune suppression for orthotopic liver transplantation due to primary biliary cirrhosis. massive lower gi bleeding in intestinal tuberculosis is uncommon and most often due to ulcerations in the terminal ileum, cecum or colon (10). there have been no reports of massive lower gi bleeding in children due to gitb. although the antral biopsy did not demonstrate pathological abnormality, the ct, us and ugi all reflect diffuse gi tract involvement. among the extrapulmonary manifestations of tuberculosis, gastrointestinal presentation is quite uncommon. a retrospective study by maltezou et al in 2000 reviewed 102 cases of extrapulmonary tuberculosis in children and found that the most common presentation was lymphadenitis (n = 48) at 47%. only 2% of the cases (n = 2) were gastrointestinal (11). in addition, most children with gitb present with vague symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, weight loss, fever and emesis. one small review of gitb in children over a 16-year period found 8 of 13 cases presented with abdominal pain and only 4 presented with fever or vomiting (12). patients can present with gitb localized to the small bowel, colon and/or peritoneal cavity. most often, gitb is located in the ileocecal area, often leading to further difficulty in differentiating it from crohn disease (13). endoscopic findings in gitb vary but include circular ulcers as were seen in our patient. other descriptions include nodules, sessile firm polyps and small diverticula (14,15). pathological diagnosis of gitb is difficult because stains are often negative for the organism and may reveal both caseating and noncaseating granulomas. gastrointestinal tuberculosis may exist without pulmonary disease as evidenced by our patient. a review by horvath and whelan in 1998 found only 20% of cases of gitb are associated with active pulmonary tuberculosis. in addition, patients with gitb may have a negative ppd. up to 14% patients with gitb have negative ppds (14). in these cases, diagnosis is made by gastric aspirates for acid-fast bacilli, tissue culture, tissue with positive ziehl-neelsen stain or polymerase chain reaction for tubercle bacilli dna (15). our patient had no significant past medical history, was immunocompetent and was hiv negative. it is unclear why an otherwise healthy child would present with such an aggressive case of gastrointestinal tuberculosis. from her endoscopy and imaging tests, we know that her disease involved portions of the small bowel and colon from the duodenum to the rectosigmoid. she also had extensive peritoneal involvement with lymphadenopathy and fluid collections. in our opinion, it is likely that her ruptured appendix may have been the first presentation of disease. ruptured appendix has been described as the initial presentation of gitb (16). review of the pathology from our patient's appendix revealed necrotizing granulomas, although special stains for acid-fast bacilli were negative. we believe the positivity for adenovirus 40/41 and rotavirus was an incidental finding and most likely had little clinical impact on her course. gastrointestinal tuberculosis is known as the great mimic and is difficult to diagnose. it is well supported in the literature that crohn disease is misdiagnosed as gitb and vice versa; this is of serious consequence because inappropriate treatment can be detrimental. the use of common immunosuppressive agents for crohn disease can cause significant morbidity in a patient with tuberculosis. timely diagnosis remains a crucial issue and is of great consequence in countries where tuberculosis is endemic and in the united states, where rates of tuberculosis peaked in the 1990s and have remained relatively high (17). a study by patel et al of 260 patients in india found that 3.9% of the patients with crohn disease were initially diagnosed with gitb (18). diagnosis of gitb remains difficult because of the nonspecific signs and symptoms at presentation and its overlap with other more common gi diseases. radiological imaging does not provide a definitive diagnosis, although ct, us or barium contrast studies may detect changes consistent with gitb. in addition, false-negative ppd tests or the lack of pulmonary involvement may further delay the diagnosis. in essence, this case serves as a reminder that gitb must be considered early in the differential diagnosis for patients with severe abdominal pain and gi bleeding of unclear etiology that may resemble crohn disease. gitb should also be included in the differential diagnosis of a patient with gi bleeding due to a vascular aneurysm. furthermore, this case illustrates that children can develop mycotic sma aneurysms that present with massive life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. acknowledgments: the authors thank dr stefano guandalini for his helpful suggestions and assistance in editing the article and dr jiri nevoral for his assistance in translating one of the references into english. we also thank dr kate feinstein and dr david yousefzadeh for their interpretation of the radiological images.

title: genealogies of orientalism and occidentalism: sephardi jews, muslims, and the americas
display_name: Genealogies of Orientalism and Occidentalism: Sephardi Jews, Muslims, and the Americas
abstract: abstract tracing orientalism back to the two 1492s of iberia and of the americas the authors examine latin america s ambivalence toward its moorish-sephardic heritage. once belonging to a shared cultural landscape, muslims and jews were later seen by ibero-american authorities as alien excrescences to be symbolically excised from a putatively pure body politic. modernization came to be synonymous with occidentalization. using gilberto freyre s work as a case study, the authors highlight his tracing of both patriarchal authoritarianism and sexual-racial flexibility in relation to brazil s moorish lineage, as well as his recuperation of the sephardi for the national formation of brazil s economy, science, and culture. freyre s revisionist project with regards to the sephardi and the moor, which offers a luso-brazilian apologia of miscegenation, must be understood in light of the omission of the enslaved african-muslims from official history. the authors outline the anxious affections that the janus-faced figure of the moor/sephardi has provoked in the americas, thus disturbing facile analytical dichotomies of east/west and north/south.

title: sounds like a broken record: preservation and access of audio-visual records at the south african broadcasting corporation radio
display_name: Sounds like a broken record: preservation and access of audio-visual records at the South African broadcasting corporation radio
abstract: purpose audio-visual records produced by public broadcasters play a role in preserving the history, culture and language of a country. the records are used by broadcasters to repeat and support programmes on air. the formats that carry these records such as tapes and compact discs are fragile and have a short life span. this is compounded by evolving technologies and results in obsolete playback equipment, which can result in records not being accessible. this study aims to explore the preservation and access of audio-visual records at the south african broadcasting corporation (sabc) radio in limpopo regional offices. design/methodology/approach qualitative data were collected through interviews from purposively selected participants in three radio stations of the sabc in the limpopo province which are munghana lonene fm, phalaphala fm and thobela fm. the interview data were augmented through participant observation. findings the findings revealed that the sabc radio archive was preserving audio-visual records in obsolete formats such as long plays and cassettes, which also lacked playback equipment. these formats were not properly arranged and were kept in a storage area that was not monitored for decaying and security. it was further established that the radio stations were using iona technology for retrieval of and access to records while the news division within the radio stations were relying on electronic news production system. as audio-visual materials were not catalogued, it proved difficult for users to access these records. practical implications this study adds value to the existing theoretical and conceptual issues that form the ongoing discourse on the preservation of and access to audio-visual records which are often neglected in the developing countries. the study also laid the groundwork for further investigation of the audio-visual records at broadcasting corporations. this is prompted by the findings which established that valuable information has been lost and continues to be lost due to poor management of audio-visual records. therefore, a further study on migration of content from analogue to digital for the purpose of continuous preservation is recommended. originality/value the study triangulated data collection tools including interviews and participant observation. the context was on the national broadcaster and the focus was on the preservation of and access to audio-visual records for the radio.
